stops.name: Princeton, spooky action at a distance
stops.campa: With his young collaborators Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen, Einstein publishes at the Institute a short paper describing a pair of particles that quantum mechanics says remain linked, however far apart they travel, so that measuring one instantly fixes the state of the other. He intends the argument, ever after called EPR, as a reductio: no sane theory of physical reality, he insists, should permit such an instantaneous, ghostly connection across empty space. Bohr's rebuttal satisfies the physics community far more than it satisfies Einstein, who goes on calling the effect, privately and for the rest of his life, spooky action at a distance, unresolved to his own satisfaction to the end.
stops.quote: No reasonable definition of reality could be expected to permit this.
stops.quote_source: Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen, 'Can Quantum-Mechanical Description of Physical Reality Be Considered Complete?', Physical Review, 1935

stops.name: Peconic, Long Island, the letter to Roosevelt
stops.campa: Vacationing in a rented cottage at Nassau Point on Long Island, Einstein is visited by his old collaborator Leo Szilard, who has come, with Edward Teller driving, to warn him that nuclear fission, newly discovered in Germany, might be turned into a weapon of terrible power before the Allies think to try. Einstein signs a letter, largely Szilard's drafting, urging President Roosevelt to fund American research into the uranium chain reaction before Berlin does; the letter, once delivered in October by the economist Alexander Sachs, becomes the seed of the Manhattan Project, though Einstein himself, refused a security clearance for his past pacifism, will never once set foot inside it.
stops.quote: This new phenomenon would also lead to the construction of bombs, and it is conceivable — though much less certain — that extremely powerful bombs of a new type may thus be constructed.
stops.quote_source: Letter to President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Peconic, Long Island, 2 August 1939

stops.name: Trenton, an American citizen
stops.campa: In the federal courthouse at Trenton, Einstein takes the oath of United States citizenship alongside his stepdaughter Margot and his devoted secretary Helen Dukas, who have made the same journey with him from Berlin. He keeps his Swiss citizenship too, unwilling to be stateless again as he was for five years after Munich, but it is as an American now, gladly and without ambivalence, that he will spend the war years advising the Navy on ordnance and buying war bonds at rallies, a stateless man's son become, of his own choosing, a citizen twice over.

stops.name: Princeton, Oppenheimer and the Institute made new
stops.campa: J. Robert Oppenheimer, fresh from directing the wartime laboratory at Los Alamos that built the weapons Einstein's letter had helped set in motion, becomes director of the Institute for Advanced Study, and the two men, so differently marked by the bomb, one who never built it and regrets the letter that started it, one who built it and cannot forget it, share the same small campus for the rest of Einstein's life. They respect each other without ever growing close; each, in his own register, becomes for the wider public the face of a physics that has learned it can end the world as easily as explain it.

stops.name: Princeton, walking home with Gödel
stops.campa: For his seventieth birthday the logician Kurt Gödel, his closest friend at the Institute though almost his opposite in temperament, gives Einstein a paper proving that Einstein's own field equations permit universes that rotate as a whole, closing time back on itself so that a traveler could in principle voyage into their own past. Einstein, increasingly isolated from a physics community that has moved on to quantum field theory he distrusts, spends his last Princeton years chasing a unified theory of gravity and electromagnetism that never succeeds, and admits privately that it is the daily walk to and from the Institute beside Gödel, arguing without deference to either man's fame, that he now comes to the office for.
stops.quote: [He confided that his] own work no longer meant much, that he came to the Institute merely to have the privilege of walking home with Gödel.
stops.quote_source: Recounted by Oskar Morgenstern, colleague at the Institute for Advanced Study

stops.name: Princeton, the presidency of Israel declined
stops.campa: On the death of Chaim Weizmann, Israel's first president, the ambassador Abba Eban delivers Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion's offer of the presidency itself to the house on Mercer Street. Einstein, seventy-three, declines by return letter, pleading a lack of the natural aptitude and the experience for dealing with people that high office would demand, though the tie to the Jewish cause he names as the strongest human bond of his life remains unbroken; Ben-Gurion, for his part, is said to have worried aloud what on earth they would have done had the old man said yes.
stops.quote: I am the more distressed over these circumstances because my relationship to the Jewish people has become my strongest human bond, ever since I became fully aware of our precarious situation among the nations of the world.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Abba Eban declining the presidency of Israel, 18 November 1952

stops.name: Princeton, the last signature, remember your humanity
stops.campa: Days before his final illness, Einstein signs, at Bertrand Russell's request, a joint manifesto with ten other eminent scientists warning that the hydrogen bomb now threatens the continued existence of the human species, and urging the world's governments to renounce war itself before some future conflict ends everything worth arguing about. It is his last public act, closing a life that began with a compass needle answering to a hidden force with a plea for humanity to answer, for once, only to its own survival.
stops.quote: Remember your humanity, and forget the rest.

stops.name: Princeton Hospital, the elegant departure
stops.campa: An abdominal aortic aneurysm, diagnosed years before and left deliberately unrepaired, bursts on the seventeenth of April; Einstein refuses the surgery that might prolong his life a little further, telling his stepdaughter Margot that he wishes to go when he wishes and to do it with some elegance. In the small hours of the eighteenth, alone with a night nurse who speaks no German, he says a few last sentences in his native tongue that she cannot understand and that no one afterward can recover; he dies before dawn. He is cremated the same day, his ashes scattered at a place he asked to remain unknown, and his brain, without family permission, is removed and kept.
stops.quote: I want to go when I want. It is tasteless to prolong life artificially; I have done my share, it is time to go. I will do it elegantly.
stops.quote_source: Reported final statement, refusing surgery, Princeton, April 1955
